newsitem.title: USA: U.S. formally proposes new car airbag rules.
newsitem.headline: U.S. formally proposes new car airbag rules.

text.p: Federal regulators on Monday formally proposed new car airbag rules to reduce the chances of the life-saving bags killing or injuring young children and frail adults in crashes.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) proposed that car-makers be authorised to reduce the power with which the bags inflate by 20-35 percent.

It said the lower power would better protect children yet inflate fast enough to protect belted and unbelted adults. The NHTSA also proposed to allow dealers and mechanics to deactivate airbags if requested by car owners.
It announced on Nov. 22 that it planned to issue the proposals following a period of public comment.
Airbags are estimated to have saved the lives of more than 1,700 people since first installed, but also to have led to the deaths of 32 children and a number of adults.
Their inflation speeds of up to 200 miles an hour can snap the neck of a child or frail adult riding in the front seat or riding unbuckled.

The NHTSA said it believed the cut in power "will reduce the incidence of injury and improve the performance of airbags for children, small stature adults and other belted occupants, while still providing significant protection for unbelted occupants."

It said the deactivation proposal provides families who need to transport children in the front seat, people with medical conditions or others concerned about airbag safety with an easier way to have the bags cut off.
Now, the NHTSA considers requests to deactivate airbags on a case-by-case medical reason basis.
The NHTSA said it expected the new regulations would go into effect in about a month and be implemented by car-makers before the start of the 1998 model year.

NHTSA Administrator Ricardo Martinez said the lower-power bags would remain in place until "smart" technology was developed that would sense when a child or small adult was in the passenger seat and lower the inflation force automatically.
He said the agency's aim was to begin to phase-in "smart" airbags in the autumn of 1998 for the 1999 model year.
The NHTSA also extended its existing policy of allowing manufacturers to install manual airbag cut-off switches in vehicles without a backseat or a backseat too small for a child safety seat.
A switch allows the driver to cut off the bag when a child is in the front seat but to turn it back on for an adult.
